subject: AI & Agents
title: Accuracy Is Not Enough
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Accuracy Is Not Enough.

hook.text: A model that predicts 'no cancer' every time is 99% accurate — because only 1% have cancer.

buildup.text: When classes are imbalanced, accuracy becomes a misleading metric.

discovery.text: Precision asks: 'Of those I flagged, how many were correct?' Recall asks: 'Of those that exist, how many did I find?'

twist.text: You can't maximize both. Catching all cancers means more false positives.

climax.text: The F1 score balances precision and recall into a single number.

punchline.text: The right metric depends on the cost of being wrong.

quiz.question: Why is accuracy alone misleading for imbalanced datasets?
options: A model can achieve high accuracy by always predicting the majority class
Accuracy always gives the same result

details.summary: Overall accuracy can be misleading when classes are imbalanced. A model could achieve 99% accuracy on cancer detection by simply predicting 'no cancer' every time if only 1% of patients have cancer.
details.whyItMatters: Relying solely on accuracy leads to dangerous blind spots. For medical, financial, and safety applications, understanding precision, recall, and F1 score is essential for responsible AI evaluation.
takeaways: High accuracy can hide failure on rare but important cases
Precision measures how many positive predictions are correct
Recall measures how many actual positives are detected

faq.question: When is accuracy a good metric?
faq.answer: When classes are roughly balanced and all types of errors are equally costly. For spam detection with 50-50 spam ratio, accuracy works fine. For rare disease detection, it is dangerously misleading.

faq.question: What metrics should be used instead of accuracy?
faq.answer: Precision, recall, and F1 score for classification. AUC-ROC for ranking models. Mean absolute error for regression. The right metric depends on whether false positives or false negatives are more costly.
